new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the word; stress is non-contrastive/predictable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary or rhythmic stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('word stress'); a two-sentence structural note in a survey-style sketch based on O'Grady's 1955 and Hale's 1960 unpublished field materials, not a dedicated prosody description. The same volume's Yulbaridja section (to which Wanman phonology is said to be otherwise identical) says 'Stress is predictable and, as in most other Australian languages, occurs on the initial syllable.' Babinski 2026 (JIPA) found no significant f0/duration correlate of initial stress in a 1-speaker, 428-vowel Warnman sample and flags that result as unreliable.
new_statements.identity_note: O'Grady, Voegelin & Voegelin 1966 describe 'Wanman /waṇman/' of the Wati subgroup, territory c. 22°S 123°E, from O'Grady 1955 and Hale 1960 field materials — the same language as Glottolog wanm1242 Warnman (AIATSIS A62, ISO wbt). No dialect specified (Thieberger 1993 notes at least two dialects, Nyarnijarra around Lake Auld and an unnamed south-western one).

sources.citation: Babinski, Sarah. 2026. Stress in Australian languages: A phonetic typology. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 56, e5, 1-28. doi:10.1017/S0025100325100832 (open access).
sources.note: Treats Warnman as one of 13 languages 'with a documented description of fixed and word initial lexical stress' (sec. 2.1) without citing a Warnman-specific description; acoustic test on 1 speaker (Thieberger, PARADISEC NT10, 131 words/428 vowels): no significant f0 or vowel-duration effect of initial stress, small intensity effect, 43.6% word-final lengthening; author flags the Warnman results as unreliable because of data size (sec. 2.5.2).
